subject: Environmental Management

source.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

outcomes.text: Name the world's continents and major oceans.
Describe the World Bank income groups: low, middle and high income economies.
Define sustainability as meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs.
Explain why resources need sustainable management.
Describe the water cycle, including condensation, precipitation, interception, infiltration, run-off, through-flow, groundwater flow, transpiration and evaporation.
Interpret and draw water cycle diagrams.

topics.title: 1.5 The structure and composition of the atmosphere

subtopics.title: Layers and gases of the atmosphere

outcomes.text: Name the major gases in the atmosphere: nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, argon and water vapour.
Describe the four atmospheric layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
State that the ozone layer sits in the stratosphere.
Describe the ozone layer and how it absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Outline the natural greenhouse effect that keeps Earth's temperature stable.
Define biome, ecosystem, population, community, habitat and niche.
Name the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem.
Describe how biotic factors affect numbers and diversity of organisms.
Outline biotic interactions: competition, grazing and predation.
Define photosynthesis as plants making glucose from carbon dioxide, water and light energy.
State the word and chemical equations for photosynthesis.
State that chlorophyll captures light energy.
Explain how water, carbon dioxide and light limit photosynthesis rate.
Explain how photosynthesis on land and in oceans forms carbon stores and affects atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Define producer, primary, secondary and tertiary consumer, and decomposer.
Define trophic levels as feeding levels in food chains.
Identify organisms at different feeding levels in a food chain or web.
State that energy passes along a food chain starting with a producer.
Explain how energy is lost in food chains through respiration and waste.
Construct simple food chains and food webs.
Define aerobic respiration as reactions in cells that break down glucose and release energy, carbon dioxide and water.
State the word and chemical equation for aerobic respiration.
Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossilisation and combustion.
Interpret and draw carbon cycle diagrams.
Describe the scientific method as the interplay of observation, hypothesis, testing and evaluation.
Form hypotheses from observations or experimental data.
Design investigations that control variables and collect quantitative results.
Explain and identify dependent and independent variables in an experiment.
Interpret data to decide if they support or refute a hypothesis.
Explain how measurement limitations cause uncertainty in results.
Explain that a hypothesis supported again and again can become a theory.

topics.title: 2.2 Environmental research in the context of climate change

outcomes.text: Define reliable and bias and explain why they matter in environmental investigations.
Using climate change examples, outline how historical data have developed.
Using climate change examples, outline how bias has led to misuse of scientific data.
Using climate change examples, outline how unreliable data caused false reporting of conclusions.
State that sampling strategies collect representative data.
Explain how random and systematic sampling spread samples well with low bias.
Explain what makes random or systematic sampling suitable: size, access and knowledge of the environment.
Evaluate the choice of random or systematic sampling in familiar and unfamiliar contexts.

topics.title: 2.4 Data collection techniques and data analysis

outcomes.text: Describe field techniques: quadrats, pitfall traps, sweep nets, beating trays, kick sampling, light traps and capture-mark-recapture.
Describe water turbidity measurement, questionnaires and interviews.
Describe the benefits and limitations of each sampling technique.
Select and use a suitable technique to collect environmental data.
Calculate estimated population size using the Lincoln index.
Calculate biodiversity using Simpson's index of diversity.
Estimate percentage cover and frequency from quadrat data.
Estimate abundance from quadrat data using a scale such as ACFOR.

topics.title: 2.5 The use of technology in data collection and analysis

outcomes.text: State that data collection can use technology: geospatial systems, satellite sensors, radio tracking, computer modelling and crowd sourcing.
Describe what is meant by big data.
Outline the benefits and limitations of analysing big data.
Plan an environmental investigation with an aim, method, data collection and processing (case study).
Calculate population density from given data.
Explain factors affecting population density and distribution: environmental, economic, social, political and historical.
Describe populations by size and age group composition.
Explain how birth, death and migration rates change population size and composition.
Define and calculate the dependency ratio.
Suggest reasons for differences between population structures of HICs and LICs.
Describe the impacts of ageing populations: lower tax revenue, higher pension spending, health care pressure and rising retirement age.
Describe and evaluate strategies for managing population change, such as contraception access, education, women's opportunities, health care and national and global policies.
Compare and contrast population dynamics of a HIC and a LIC (case study).
Describe the major terrestrial biomes by climate, soil and vegetation: desert, forest, grassland and tundra.
Outline primary and secondary succession from pioneer species to a climax community.
Define gross primary productivity and net primary productivity.
Define ecosystem productivity as the rate of biomass production.
Discuss the efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels.
Interpret and draw ecological pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy.
Explain the shapes of ecological pyramids.
Define native and invasive species.
Explain the impacts of invasive species on biodiversity.
Describe and explain the benefits of conserving biodiversity: medicines, resources, genes, ecological services and cultural value.
Describe and evaluate legislation and protocols for conservation, such as CITES, IWC, EU CFP, ITTO and the IUCN Red List.
Describe and explain the role of the EDGE programme.
Describe and evaluate captive breeding and release.
Describe and evaluate habitat conservation and creation, including rewilding, reserves, protected areas and national parks.

topics.title: 4.3 Impacts of human activity on ecosystems

outcomes.text: Describe and explain human impacts on tropical rainforests, such as deforestation, timber, farming, mining and reservoirs.
Describe and evaluate strategies for managing rainforest impacts: legislation, sustainable harvesting, debt-for-nature swaps and protected areas.
Describe and explain human impacts on Antarctica: climate change, ozone depletion, tourism, overfishing, mineral extraction and research.
Describe and evaluate strategies for managing Antarctic impacts, such as the Antarctic Treaty and protected areas.
Evaluate strategies to conserve the biodiversity of a named ecosystem (case study).
Define food security as everyone having access to enough safe, nutritious food for a healthy life.
Describe and explain causes of food insecurity, such as population growth, land degradation, disease, biofuels, climate change, water shortage and poverty.
Outline the impacts of food insecurity: scarcity, malnutrition, poverty, forced migration, conflict, famine and death.
Describe and evaluate ways to raise food production: subsistence farming, intensification and extensification.
Evaluate improved techniques: aquaculture, hydroponics, selective breeding, GM crops, fertilisers, herbicides, fungicides and biological control.
Evaluate other strategies: more crops and fewer livestock, less food waste, stockpiling, better transport, protecting pollinators, food aid and rationing.
Classify energy resources as renewable or non-renewable.
Define energy security as reliable, affordable energy supply with environmental impacts considered.
Distinguish long-term from short-term energy security.
Describe and explain causes of energy insecurity, such as fuel depletion, uneven resources, population growth, climate change and supply disruption.
Outline the impacts of energy insecurity on supply, prices, jobs, poverty, imports and conflict.
Describe and evaluate strategies for energy security: efficiency, more production, renewables, new technology, local projects and rationing.
Describe waste disposal and treatment: landfill, incineration, storage, disposal at sea, recycling and exporting waste.
Explain the impacts of disposal methods: leaching, methane, pollution, disease, toxins, bioaccumulation and ocean plastics.
Describe and evaluate strategies to reduce waste impacts: reduce, reuse, recycle, biodegradable plastics, composting and energy from waste.
Evaluate education, financial incentives and legislation as ways to cut waste.
Compare the impacts of future energy insecurity on a HIC and a LIC (case study).
Describe how Earth's water is distributed: oceans, surface fresh water, sub-surface water and atmosphere.
Define water security as access to enough clean water for food, goods, sanitation and health care.
Explain the causes of water insecurity, including climate change, disasters, pollution, population growth and competing demands.
Explain the impacts of water insecurity, including crop failure, food shortage and water-borne illness.
Describe and evaluate ways to extract and supply water sustainably: pipes, wells, boreholes, reservoirs and dams.
Describe and evaluate ways to reduce water use: better irrigation, less thirsty crops, recycling and rain catchment.
Evaluate education, poverty reduction, international agreement, aid and rationing.
Study the impacts of water insecurity on a region and evaluate its water strategies (case study).
Define acid deposition as acidic wet deposition (pH below 5.6) or dry deposition.
Describe the two types: wet deposition (rain, snow, hail, fog) and dry deposition (dust, gases).
Outline how acid deposition forms from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Outline impacts on aquatic environments, vegetation and crops, and buildings.
Define photochemical smog formed when nitrogen oxides and VOCs react in sunlight.
Describe its impacts: irritation, lower crop yields and damaged plastics and rubber.

Describe strategies for managing air pollution: less fossil fuel use, desulfurisation, catalytic converters, precipitators, VOC control, vehicle limits and legislation including the polluter pays principle.

subtopics.title: How the ozone layer is depleted

outcomes.text: Outline how CFCs reach the stratosphere and release chlorine that destroys ozone.
State that ozone is measured in Dobson Units.
Define the ozone hole as an area below 100 Dobson Units.
Explain why ozone depletion has been greatest over Antarctica.
Describe the impacts of ozone depletion on health, crops, ecosystems and materials.
Evaluate international agreements to phase out ozone-depleting substances.
Outline the impacts of alternatives such as HCFCs and F-gases.
Outline the importance of experimental evidence using the Rowland-Molina hypothesis.
Evaluate the management of a named atmospheric pollution event (case study).
Define greenhouse gases and identify carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane.
State major human sources: fossil fuel combustion, rice fields, livestock and landfill.
Explain how more greenhouse gases cause the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.
Outline the difficulties of monitoring and predicting climate change.
State the impacts of climate change on the environment: temperature, rainfall, sea level, circulation, melting ice and biodiversity.
Describe the impacts on people: extreme weather, property damage, migration, crop yields and food, energy and water security.
Describe ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions, from lifestyle changes and low-carbon energy to carbon capture, forests, efficient buildings and adaptation.
Describe agreements such as the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement.
Outline geo-engineering strategies such as solar radiation management.
Evaluate strategies for managing climate change, and the impacts on a named location (case study).
